cues.en: I've got my myocardial-themed tea ready because today we're going to talk about fake disease. We're living in the era of fake news after all, so it's only fitting. And I'm not talking about selfieitis or affluenza. I mean things like cancer. So what am I going on about? Well, this episode is about when cancer isn't cancer. Have you ever thought about getting one of those full body scans? You know the kind. A very emotive advert, perhaps on the train with a...
cues.zh: 我已经备好了我的“心肌”主题茶，因为今天我们要聊聊“假疾病”。毕竟我们生活在一个假新闻满天飞的时代，聊这个再合适不过了。我说的可不是“自拍成瘾症”或“富裕病”，我说的是像癌症这类疾病。我到底在讲什么？这期视频讲的就是“当癌症并不是癌症”的情况。你有没有考虑过去做个全身扫描？你知道我说的是哪种。往往是那种极其煽情的广告，可能是在火车上，画面里有……

cues.en: grieving wife and children. If only that dead fool had come in for our cancer screening service, he'd still be with his family today. They work on scaremongering, and pretty much make it sound like it's almost your fault if you get some horrible disease because you simply weren't paying close enough attention to your health.
cues.zh: 悲痛欲绝的妻儿。要是那个死鬼当初来做我们的癌症筛查，今天就能继续陪在家人身边了。这类广告靠制造恐慌来牟利，而且听起来就像是在说：你要是得了什么可怕的重病，那全是你自己的错，谁让你平时不够关注自己的健康呢。

cues.en: And that's why you should spend $9.99.99. Now, I'm not gonna tell you what to do with your money, but I'm certainly not going to spend any of my own on a well-manned checkup or full-body scan, and I'll try to explain why. The concepts in this video are some of the hardest to grasp in the whole of medicine, so I'm not gonna try and cover too much in this video, and I'm sure we can revisit things in future videos. Some of the things you'll hear will sound completely contradictory and counterintuitive. We'll start with Kevin Hart.
cues.zh: 所以你才该掏出这999.99美元。我不会对你怎么花钱指手画脚，但我自己是绝对不会把钱花在健康体检或全身扫描上的，我尽量来解释一下原因。这个视频里的概念在整个医学界都属于最难理解的一类，所以我不会一口气讲太多，以后的视频里我们肯定还会再聊。你接下来听到的某些内容可能会显得极其矛盾、反直觉。我们先从 Kevin Hart 讲起。

cues.en: who watches a news report about how many men his age are dropping down dead from heart disease. He sees a documentary about a CT scan that can detect early narrowing of the arteries before you have any symptoms. He pays handsomely for a cardiac CT scan, which finds a 70% narrowing in a coronary artery, which the reporting doctor calls a ticking time bomb.
cues.zh: 他看到一则新闻报道，讲的是有多少跟他同龄的男性因心脏病突发猝死。他又看了一部纪录片，介绍某种 CT 扫描能在出现任何症状之前就检测出动脉早期狭窄。于是他花了大价钱做了一次心脏 CT 扫描，查出冠状动脉有70%的狭窄，出具报告的医生把它称为“定时炸弹”。

cues.en: He undergoes the implantation of a stent, which is a procedure where we insert a tiny metal tube about the diameter of the spring inside your biro, but with much thinner metal. Unfortunately, he suffers quite extensive bleeding in his right arm, which gets very swollen and he has to stay in hospital for a couple of days and can't drive for a month. But after all that, he's okay. Next up, we've got Mary Mellon.
cues.zh: 他接受了支架植入手术，这个手术会在血管里置入一根微型金属管，直径大概和圆珠笔里的弹簧差不多，但金属壁要薄得多。不幸的是，他的右臂出现了严重出血，肿得非常厉害，不得不住院观察几天，并且整整一个月不能开车。但经历这一切之后，他没什么大碍了。接下来是 Mary Mellon 的故事。

cues.en: A 45-year-old woman who hears that breast screening saves lives. She attends for mammography. A government-run program, so paid for by taxes. It's a very uncomfortable test, but she soldiers through because she feels it's important, and is shocked to hear an abnormality was found. She has a biopsy which shows ductal carcinoma in situ, a type of cancer.
cues.zh: 她是一位45岁的女性，听说乳腺筛查能挽救生命。于是她去做了乳腺钼靶检查。这是政府主导的项目，由税收出资。检查过程非常难受，但她觉得这很重要，还是咬牙挺了过来，结果却震惊地得知发现了异常。随后的活检结果显示为导管原位癌，这是一种癌症。

cues.en: She's got two young children. She's terrified and opts to have a complete mastectomy, along with an unpleasant course of chemotherapy. She develops an infection of the surgical area. It takes a while to heal, and she's left with permanent swelling of her left arm. But after all that, she's okay. So how do you think Kevin and Mary feel? Alright, their operations had some complications, but at the end of the day, they're alive. They feel like their lives have been saved.
cues.zh: 她还有两个年幼的孩子。她吓坏了，选择接受全乳房切除术，同时还做了一个疗程痛苦的化疗。术后她的手术部位发生了感染，养了很久才愈合，而且左臂留下了永久性水肿。但经历这一切之后，她好歹挺过来了。那你觉得 Kevin 和 Mary 现在是什么心情？好吧，他们的手术确实出现了一些并发症，但说到底，他们还活着，并且都觉得自己捡回了一条命。

cues.en: families are overjoyed, their diseases were caught early. They probably feel tremendous gratitude and are likely to recommend the test to all their friends and family and who can blame them, especially when the doctors themselves often reinforce this belief. But is what they believe
cues.zh: 家属们欣喜若狂，因为疾病被早期发现了。他们大概会万分感激，也很可能把这项检查推荐给所有亲友——这也不能怪他们，尤其医生自己也常常强化这种看法。但他们所相信的

cues.en: actually true. In both cases, we know that, in fact, the likely outcome of them undergoing those initial tests is that they've been harmed more than they've benefited. We know that for stable, asymptomatic patients like Kevin, stents do not prolong life, nor reduce the likelihood of having a heart attack. And in fact, I don't think anybody would put a stent in Kevin today, but this scenario would have been very common a few years ago. Don't get me wrong.
cues.zh: 真的成立吗？在这两种情况下，我们都知道，实际上他们接受那些初始检查后，更可能的结果是受到的伤害大于获益。我们知道，对于像 Kevin 这样病情稳定、无症状的患者，支架既不能延长寿命，也不能降低心脏病发作的可能性。事实上，我觉得今天没人会给 Kevin 放支架，但几年前这种情况会非常常见。别误会。

cues.en: For unstable patients, people having chest pain, people having heart attacks, stents are life-saving and one of the best therapies we have in medicine, in fact, but not for patients like Kevin. For Mary, the biopsy did show cancer, but it's a cancer that might never have caused her any symptoms whatsoever. And potentially, she had her breast removed and developed this long-term arm swelling for no net gain.
cues.zh: 对于不稳定患者——有胸痛的人、发生心脏病发作的人——支架能救命，事实上也是医学中我们拥有的最好疗法之一，但不适用于 Kevin 这样的患者。对 Mary 来说，活检确实显示了癌症，但那是一种可能永远不会引起她任何症状的癌症。而她可能切除了乳房，还出现了长期手臂肿胀，却没有净获益。

cues.en: If both of those last two paragraphs sound confusing, don't worry, just stay with me. If you have a pain and come to see me as your doctor and I send off a test, that's called investigation. That's me trying to find a cause for your symptoms. But if you don't have any symptoms, you feel completely fine, like Kevin and Mary did, and then I send off a test, that's called screening. Screening is where we try to look for the signs of a problem before a patient has any symptoms. However...
cues.zh: 如果最后两段听起来让人困惑，别担心，跟着我往下听。如果你有疼痛，作为你的医生来找我，我开一项检查，这叫病因检查。那是我在试图为你的症状寻找原因。但如果你没有任何症状，感觉完全正常，像 Kevin 和 Mary 那样，然后我开一项检查，这叫筛查。筛查是在患者出现任何症状之前，尝试寻找问题的迹象。然而……

cues.en: Unfortunately, screening is a very complicated topic, and often one that's quite emotive as well and therefore difficult to discuss. So today we're just going to talk about two concepts, lead time bias and over-diagnosis. Let's start with how we talk about disease prognosis. You've all seen that cliched conversation in movies where the protagonist says, duck, be honest with me, how long do I have? And the doctor solemnly replies, you have only six months to live. Yes.
cues.zh: 不幸的是，筛查是一个非常复杂的话题，而且常常很情绪化，因此很难讨论。所以今天我们只谈两个概念：领先时间偏倚和过度诊断。先从我们如何谈论疾病预后说起。你们都见过电影里那种老套对话：主角说，医生，跟我说实话，我还能活多久？然后医生郑重地回答：你只剩六个月可活了。是的。

cues.en: Probably don't watch as much Nigerian cinema as I do, but you get the idea. In reality, it doesn't work like that, because everybody's different. In fact, surveys of palliative care doctors who deal with death more than anybody else show that even they are spectacularly bad at predicting when a person with an illness will die. Instead, we talk about populations.
cues.zh: 你们可能没我看过那么多尼日利亚电影，但你明白意思。现实中并不是那样运作的，因为每个人都不一样。事实上，对姑息治疗医生的调查——他们比任何人都更多面对死亡——显示，即使是他们也极其不擅长预测一个患病的人何时会死。相反，我们谈论的是人群。

cues.en: So we say if you take a hundred people with this particular cancer, then in five years time, 80 of them on average will be alive. Now this is a statistic called five year survival, which is used very commonly, but it's misleading.
cues.zh: 所以我们会说，如果你取一百个患这种特定癌症的人，那么五年后，平均其中八十人还活着。现在这是一个叫五年生存率的统计指标，它被非常普遍地使用，但具有误导性。

cues.en: Rudy Giuliani, some years ago, was trying to explain why he felt American privatized health care was superior to the British National Health Service, which is free at the point of access. And he said,
cues.zh: 几年前，Rudy Giuliani 试图解释为什么他觉得美国私有化的医疗体系优于英国国家医疗服务体系（NHS，就医时免费）。他说道：

cues.en: Now that sounds like a pretty clear demonstration that the aggressive screening program for prostate cancer in America has saved many, many lives. But the death rate from prostate cancer in the UK and the US was pretty much identical.
cues.zh: 这听起来像是一个很有力的证明，表明美国针对前列腺癌的激进筛查项目挽救了无数生命。但实际上，英美两国的男性前列腺癌死亡率几乎完全一致。

cues.en: So how can both statements be true? Let's say that this is the point at which prostate cancer causes symptoms and is diagnosed. And here is when the average man dies. When we hear five year survival rates have improved due to screening, we assume it's because people are dying later. But actually, it's because we're diagnosing them earlier.
cues.zh: 那么这两种说法怎么可能同时成立呢？假设这里是前列腺癌出现症状并被确诊的时间点。而这里是患者的平均死亡时间。当我们听说筛查提高了五年生存率时，我们总以为是因为大家活得更久了。但实际上，只是因为确诊时间提前了而已。

cues.en: If you diagnose someone here, even though they're dying at the exact same time, you've not helped them in any way, their survival time from diagnosis is better, simply because you've diagnosed them earlier. This is lead time bias, and it's frequently misused to show that screening works. In fact, the correlation coefficient between five-year survival and death for the most common cancers was looked at, and it was zero. And that's really saying something.
cues.zh: 如果你在这里就确诊了某人，哪怕他们的死亡时间完全没变，你也没能帮到他们分毫，但确诊后的生存时间却看起来变长了，仅仅是因为确诊得更早。这就是前置时间偏倚（lead time bias），它经常被滥用来证明筛查有效。事实上，有人研究过最常见癌症的五年生存率与实际死亡率之间的相关系数，结果是零。这很能说明问题。

cues.en: There's no link between five-year survival and how many people are dying from a disease, which is of course the thing that any sufferer cares about, so we should just stop using five-year survival and focus on mortality. It seems like common sense to think that earlier diagnosis equals earlier effective treatment, and of course sometimes that is true. But the big problem is that our treatments are far from perfect, and in fact a lot of them are harmful in themselves, or the tests that we...
cues.zh: 五年生存率与因该疾病死亡的人数之间没有任何关联，而死亡人数才是患者真正关心的，所以我们应该停止拿五年生存率说事，把重心放在死亡率上。常识上大家都会觉得早发现等于早治疗、早见效，有时确实如此。但最大的问题在于，现有的治疗手段远谈不上完美，事实上很多治疗本身就有危害，或者在初筛之后……

cues.en: do after that initial test might be as well. And another huge challenge is you're going to end up treating a lot of fake disease. And by that I mean an abnormality that's been detected on a test that is not causing and would not cause that patient any problems whatsoever. This is over diagnosis and it's becoming more and more common as our tests are becoming more sensitive and we're able to pick up abnormalities that we would have never previously been able to detect.
cues.zh: 所做的进一步检查同样有害。另一个巨大的挑战是，你最终会治疗很多“假性疾病”。我指的是检查中发现的异常，但它其实根本没有、也绝不会给患者带来任何健康问题。这就是过度诊断，随着检测手段越来越灵敏，我们能发现以前根本查不出的异常，过度诊断也变得越来越普遍。

cues.en: Here are five of the most common cancers in the US, all of which are routinely screened for or being picked up as incidental findings in body scans. You'll see that over the last 40 years, the number of cancers being diagnosed has gone up across the board, but the lower lines, deaths from those cancers have remained remarkably stable. So either our treatments are getting better at exactly the same rate as the increase in cases, or we're diagnosing things that aren't causing any harm, aka
cues.zh: 这是美国最常见的五种癌症，它们要么是常规筛查项目，要么是在身体扫描中偶然被发现的。你可以看到，在过去的 40 年里，确诊癌症的人数全线飙升，但下面的那条线——这些癌症的死亡人数，却保持得惊人平稳。所以，要么是我们的治疗水平提升速度刚好与病例增长速度完全同步，要么就是我们在诊断一些根本无害的东西，也就是

cues.en: fake disease. In fact just last month a large and important trial was published looking at lung cancer screening. Now lung cancer is one of the most deadly diseases killing millions of people around the world and it's the kind of thing you really hope a screening program would work for but in response to the question does lung cancer screening save lives the answer was a clear no. The patients who were screened and had their lung cancer diagnosed earlier
cues.zh: “假性疾病”。事实上，就在上个月，一项针对肺癌筛查的大型重要试验发表了结果。肺癌是致死率最高的疾病之一，在全球夺走了数百万人的生命，这正是你极度希望筛查能发挥作用的病种，但对于“肺癌筛查能挽救生命吗”这个问题，答案却是明确的“不能”。那些接受了筛查并更早确诊肺癌的患者，

cues.en: had more scans, more invasive tests and more treatment like chemo and radiotherapy, but no difference in death rate. On that point, I want to briefly mention the Apple Watch because I've made a couple of videos about it and make a little comparison here. So in this trial, patients at high risk smokers were screened for a deadly disease, lung cancer, and no benefit was found. The Apple Watch looks for atrial fibrillation, which is a much less
cues.zh: 做了更多的扫描、更多侵入性检查，接受了更多化疗和放疗等治疗，但死亡率却毫无差别。说到这里，我想顺便提一下 Apple Watch，因为我做过几个关于它的视频，在这里正好做个对比。在这项试验中，吸烟这类高危人群针对肺癌这种致命疾病进行了筛查，结果没有发现任何益处。而 Apple Watch 监测的是房颤，相比肺癌，

cues.en: deadly disease than lung cancer, and the people wearing the Apple Watch on the whole are at a very low risk of atrial fibrillation. So while I've made it clear that I think the potential for what we can do with the Apple Watch is very exciting, and it's a fantastic technology, when I say that it's unlikely to save lives, I'm normally met with complete incredulity.
cues.zh: 房颤的致命性要低得多，而且佩戴 Apple Watch 的人群整体上发生房颤的风险也极低。虽然我已经明确表示过，我认为 Apple Watch 能实现的应用潜力非常令人兴奋，也是一项了不起的技术，但每当我指出它不太可能挽救生命时，大家通常都会觉得完全不可思议。

cues.en: Okay, here's another way to look at it. This is adapted from H. Gilbert Welsh's teaching on screening. Please do check the references below as I put some extra reading there, especially that of H. Gilbert Welsh and Margaret McCartney, two fantastic writers and two heroes of mine in this field, which I really recommend. Let's say a cancerous process starts here, some nasty genetic mutation or fault of cell division. Along the y-axis, we have size of the cancer. At a given size,
cues.zh: 好，我们可以换个角度来看。这借鉴了 H. Gilbert Welsh 关于癌症筛查的教学。请务必查看下方的参考资料，我放了一些延伸阅读，特别是 H. Gilbert Welsh 和 Margaret McCartney 的作品，他们是两位出色的作者，也是我在该领域的偶像，非常推荐大家去读。假设癌变从这里开始，源于某种恶性基因突变或细胞分裂异常。纵轴 y 轴代表癌症的大小。当达到某个特定大小时，

cues.en: the cancer will cause symptoms to the patient. And then, at another size, it will cause death. The x-axis is time, and over on the right is where the patient dies of a non-cancer cause, so the time they would die if they never got cancer. This is a fast-growing cancer which causes death not long after its first notice by the patient. These are not picked up with screening normally, as there's not much chance to catch them, and as you might imagine, they have a poor prognosis.
cues.zh: 癌症会让患者出现症状。而到了另一个大小时，就会导致死亡。横轴 x 轴代表时间，最右侧是患者因非癌症原因死亡的时间点，也就是如果他们从未患癌本该去世的时间。这是一种快速生长的癌症，患者初次察觉后不久就会致死。这类癌症通常很难通过筛查发现，因为能抓住它的机会非常渺茫，正如大家所料，它们的预后往往很差。

cues.en: Here we see a cancer growing at a medium rate. It eventually will cause death earlier than the patient would have otherwise lived, so this is the type of cancer you want to pick up with screening. But there's another kind of cancer. This is a very slow-growing cancer, which the patient dies with, but not from. And this is an important phrase in medicine. If you look down a microscope, the cells have all the hallmarks of cancer, but it's not cancer
cues.zh: 这里我们看到的是一种中速生长的癌症。它最终导致患者死亡的时间，早于患者原本能活的时间，所以这正是我们希望通过筛查发现的癌症类型。但还有另一种癌症。这是一种生长极其缓慢的癌症，患者是“带着它死去”，而不是“死于它”。这是医学上的一句名言。如果放到显微镜下看，这些细胞具备癌症的一切特征，但它却并不是

cues.en: in the way that you or I or society understands it. This is cancer that isn't cancer, at least not with a big C. The classic example of this is prostate cancer, which about half of older men have when they die of another cause, and it's only detected on post-mortem. Thyroid cancer rates in people who die of other causes is similar. And yet more types of cancer do this. They just sit there. Mary's ductal carcinoma and situ might go in this group. And some even regress.
cues.zh: 你、我或大众通常理解的那种癌症。这是一种“不算癌症的癌症”，至少不是通常意义上的恶性大病。最典型的例子就是前列腺癌，约半数死于其他原因的老年男性体内都存在，且仅在尸检中才能发现。死于其他原因的人群中，甲状腺癌的检出率也类似。还有更多类型的癌症也是如此。它们就只是待在那里。Mary 所患的导管原位癌可能就属于这一类。甚至有些还会自行消退。

cues.en: In fact, some people don't even call what Mary had a cancer, even though on a cellular level it definitely is. If your screening test identifies any of these, that's over-diagnosis. Disease from the Latin literally meaning without ease is not present if the pathology is not causing any symptoms nor adversely affecting the person's life. So this is what I mean by fake disease. Treating these will not only not help
cues.zh: 事实上，有些人甚至都不把 Mary 患的这种病称为癌症，尽管在细胞层面上它确实是。如果筛查检测出了这类病变，那就是“过度诊断”。Disease（疾病）源自拉丁语，字面意思是“不适、不安”；如果病理改变既不引发任何症状，也没有对生活造成负面影响，那么这种“疾病”其实并不存在。这就是我所说的“伪疾病”。治疗这些不仅帮不到

cues.en: the patient, but may even harm them, which is the one thing that doctors are definitely not supposed to do. But of course, when you're over on the left side of the graph, it's impossible to predict the trajectory of which of those lines the cancer in question will follow. So of course, you end up treating all of them. And patients with fake disease confuse the statistics like this.
cues.zh: 患者，反而可能对他们造成伤害，而这恰恰是医生最不应该做的事。但当然，当你处于图表左侧的初始阶段时，根本无法预测眼前这个癌症会顺着哪条线发展。所以理所当然地，大家最终只能把它们全部治一遍。而患有“伪疾病”的患者，就会像这样混淆统计数据。

cues.en: If you have a hundred patients with a particular cancer, in five years time, 50% of them are alive, that's a survival rate of 50%. But with screening, you may pick up another hundred who have fake disease. And now you've got 200 patients to start with. In five years time, 50 are still dead. You haven't prevented a single death, but you can immediately claim that survival rate is now 75% because 150 patients are still alive at five years.
cues.zh: 假设有100名某种癌症患者，五年后有50%存活，生存率就是50%。但如果做了筛查，你可能会多查出100个其实没病的人。这样基数就变成了200人。五年后，依然死了50人。你其实一个人都没多救，但却能立刻宣称生存率变成了75%，因为五年后还有150人活着。

cues.en: Great success. In these ducks like a quack videos, I often talk about the power of anecdote, normally as a problematic thing. For example, if I show you a meta-analysis of coagulated casein genuflection and its effect on self-reported tibiofemoral intraarticular pain, you'll probably glaze over. But if I slap some America's Got Talent sob story music on in the background and
cues.zh: “大获成功”。在我这些打假庸医的视频里，我经常会提到个案故事的影响力，通常都是作为负面问题来谈的。比如，我要是给你看一篇关于“凝固酪蛋白跪拜疗法对自述胫股关节内疼痛影响”的荟萃分析，你大概率会两眼放空。但要是我在背景里放上《美国达人秀》那种催泪煽情音乐，

cues.en: tell you about my crippling knee pain that was ignored for years by the uncaring, heartless medical profession until I built a church made of cheese and knelt at its cheddar altar every night until my knee pain was miraculously cured. Now you're interested. Oh God of cheese, hear my prayer. So I thought I'd join in with an anecdote of my own, particularly because I'm aware that my attitude is
cues.zh: 跟你讲讲我那折磨人的严重膝痛，多年来一直被冷漠无情的医疗界忽视，直到我建了一座奶酪教堂，每天晚上在切达干酪祭坛前下跪，奇迹般治愈了膝痛。这下你就有兴趣了。“哦奶酪之神，听听我的祈祷吧。”所以我想我也来讲个自己的亲身经历，尤其是我很清楚自己的态度

cues.en: completely opposite to celebrities you'll see on TV, acting as patrons for various charities, saying that their disease or cancer was caught just in the nick of time, so make sure you get screened. And by the way, I'm not attacking those celebrities at all. Kudos to them for doing a good thing. If screening is misunderstood by many in the medical profession, then it's unfair to expect anything different from non-medics. Incidentaloma is the name given to an unexpected finding on a scan.
cues.zh: 和你在电视上看到的那些明星完全相反——他们作为各类慈善机构的代言人，总在呼吁“幸好我的病或癌症发现得早，大家一定要去做筛查”。顺便说一句，我绝不是在攻击那些明星，他们做好事值得称赞。如果连很多医务人员都对筛查存在误解，那要求非医务人员搞明白显然是不公平的。所谓“意外瘤”（Incidentaloma），是指扫描检查中意外发现的病变，

cues.en: in a tissue or an organ that was normally not the intended target of the test. As the number of radiology tests we're requesting is increasing, as the scans themselves are getting more and more sensitive, the rate of incidentalomas is soaring. The most commonly requested tests, things like CT scans of the chest and abdomen, or something that I report, a cardiac MRI scan, account for loads of these incidentalomas. Cardiac MRI is now the number two source of incidentalomas
cues.zh: 它通常出现在本来并非检查目标的组织或器官里。随着我们开具的放射科检查越来越多，扫描技术本身也越来越灵敏，意外瘤的检出率正在飙升。最常开的检查，比如胸部和腹部 CT，或者我负责出报告的心脏 MRI，就查出了大量的意外瘤。心脏 MRI 目前是意外瘤的第二大来源，

cues.en: in the US. A kydec MRI is where we use an MRI machine to scan the heart, but because the heart is in the middle of the chest you get all the surrounding structures, so top of the kidneys, liver, lungs, and the thyroid, which is just here in the neck. I was reporting the scan of a 42 year old woman who I'll call Sophie, who initially presented with a very non-worrying, innocent sounding history of palpitation, fluttering heart.
cues.zh: 在美国尤其如此。心脏 MRI 是用 MRI 机器扫描心脏，但由于心脏位于胸部正中，你也会扫到周围所有的结构，比如肾脏上端、肝脏、肺部，以及脖子这里的甲状腺。当时我正在看一份42岁女性的扫描报告，姑且叫她 Sophie 吧，她最初就诊的症状听起来完全不严重，只是心悸、心慌。

cues.en: and her heart was completely normal on the scan, but I spotted something in her thyroid gland, which, as I'm not a specialist, I referred on, and this led to what's called a cascade of care. She had blood tests, she had further scans, she had a biopsy of the thyroid gland, which is where we stick a needle into the neck, and that was inconclusive, so she had to have the test repeated. It showed some concerning changes for cancer.
cues.zh: 扫描显示她的心脏完全正常，但我在她的甲状腺里发现了点东西。因为我不是专科医生，就转诊了，这引出了所谓的一连串诊疗。她做了血液检查，又做了进一步扫描，还做了甲状腺活检——就是把针扎进颈部——结果不确定，所以她不得不重做检查。检查显示有一些提示癌症的可疑变化。

cues.en: So now she's got this scary label of thyroid cancer when she only went in to see her GP in the first place for some Fluttering heartbeats which have now completely resolved. She's told she needs an operation which she undergoes She has part of her thyroid gland removed But unfortunately her recurrent laryngeal nerve which supplies the voice box is damaged Sophie then has radioactive iodine treatment as part of the ongoing therapy of her thyroid cancer which
cues.zh: 所以现在她背上了甲状腺癌这个可怕的标签，而她最初去看全科医生，只是因为心悸，现在已经完全好了。她被告知需要手术，也接受了手术，切除了部分甲状腺。但不幸的是，支配喉部的喉返神经受损了。随后Sophie接受了放射性碘治疗，作为她甲状腺癌持续治疗的一部分，而这种治疗

cues.en: is generally quite safe but has one major side effect. Now Sophie is a singer. She'd had a pretty exciting life touring the world as a backup singer for various groups and had never planned on settling down. But recently she met a guy and they had settled down and then decided to have kids. And she knew full well that at the age of 42 it was pretty late. But for the last year her fiancé and her had been trying. But then when this came along...
cues.zh: 通常相当安全，但有一个主要副作用。Sophie是个歌手。她曾过着相当精彩的生活，作为多个组合的伴唱歌手环游世界，从没打算安定下来。但最近她遇到一个男人，他们安定下来，然后决定要孩子。她很清楚，42岁已经相当晚了。但过去一年，她和未婚夫一直在尝试。可就在这时，这件事出现了……

cues.en: The thing with radioactive iodine is that you mustn't get pregnant. Add to that her voice never recovered from the operation, which obviously as a singer was devastating. Her thyroid became underactive so she has to take replacement medications and she'll be on those for life. With all this going on, not only the radioactive iodine but the whole stress of the situation, she lost a year and she feels that that was her last chance to try to get pregnant.
cues.zh: 放射性碘的问题在于，你不能怀孕。再加上她的声音手术后一直没恢复，对歌手来说这显然是毁灭性的。她的甲状腺功能减退了，所以必须服用替代药物，而且终身都要吃。这一切叠加在一起——不只是放射性碘，还有整件事的压力——让她耽误了一年，她觉得那是她最后一次尝试怀孕的机会。

cues.en: I could have picked a very black and white story where an incidental omo was picked up that was definitely not harmful and the patient underwent a litany of tests and horrendous complications. And believe me, every medic knows a story like that. But I chose this one because it's actually had an impact on me. I don't know if...
cues.zh: 我本可以讲一个非黑即白的故事：偶然发现了一个绝对无害的偶发瘤，结果病人接受了一连串检查，还遭遇了可怕的并发症。相信我，每个医生都见过这样的故事。但我选了这个，因为它确实对我有触动。我不知道是否……

cues.en: The thyroid cancer would have killed Sophie, perhaps it would, perhaps it was for the best that she went through all of that in spite of the complications. I'll never have the answer to whether that thyroid cancer should have come out or not, and neither will Sophie. And that uncertainty, unfortunately, is central to everything we do in medicine. Our tests are not perfect. They produce false positives. But even when the results are genuine, it's not always entirely clear what we do with that information.
cues.zh: 那个甲状腺癌本来可能会要了Sophie的命——也许确实会；也许尽管有这些并发症，她经历这一切反而是最好的结果。我永远无法知道那个甲状腺癌到底该不该被切除，Sophie也永远不会知道。而遗憾的是，这种不确定性正是我们医学工作一切的核心。我们的检查并不完美，会产生假阳性。但即使结果是真的，我们也并不总能完全清楚该拿这些信息怎么办。

cues.en: I can only apologise to you as the public that you get such conflicting messages about things like screening. And as I said at the beginning of this video, I am not suggesting to anybody watching not to have a screening test. But hopefully now you can make a more informed decision. I'm on my way to work. Back to the Grind for a few magical days in a company of some of the best educational YouTubers out there, imbibing their wisdom.
cues.zh: 关于像筛查这类事情，大家会接收到如此矛盾的信息，作为公众的一员，我只能向大家深表歉意。正如我在本期视频开头所说，我绝不是建议任何观众不要去做筛查测试。但希望现在大家能做出更明智的决定。我正在去上班的路上。回到日常的忙碌中，此前我和一批顶尖的教育类 YouTuber 共度了奇妙的几天，汲取了他们的智慧。

cues.en: just basking in the aura of their edutuber magnificence. People like Wendover, RealLife Law, Kuzgizar, TGP Grey, Ali Abdaal, Science with Katie, Knowing Better, and many more. Because it was YouTube EDUCON, a meeting of all those educational YouTubers and lots of others from around the globe. And due to some bizarre administrative cock up, I found myself hosting the whole event.

cues.en: along with the fantastic Maddie Mote. And I told a joke that Philip Detmer of Cuzgasag described as the greatest joke ever told at a YouTube event to date and probably forevermore. But I guess you had to be there. Enough showing off. The reason I'm bringing this up is because you'll find all of the aforementioned educational YouTubers on Nebula, which...
